title: Stride-aware weight sharding throughput probe
content:
Purpose and quick summary:

This note captures an exploratory probe into how different weight-shard placement strategies (what I call stride-aware sharding) interact with pipeline/tensor parallel execution and interconnect/NCCL behavior. The goal was to identify easily actionable placement heuristics that increase sustained throughput for common decoding workloads (autoregressive sampling, top-k/top-p) without increasing tail latency.

Why this came up (context):
- We observed non-deterministic throughput gaps across identical cluster hardware when rolling out a new quantized model. Some pods hit ~14k tokens/s, others ~10k tokens/s under same QPS and batch sizing.
- Flamegraphs showed surprising host-to-device staging bursts and periodic AllReduce stalls not explained by NVLink bisection alone.
- Hypothesis: the logical weight shard stride (how consecutive tensor shards are mapped to device indices) can create pathological cross-node link contention and longer NCCL ring hops under our hybrid TP/DP topologies.

High-level experiment plan:
1) Microbench: single-step forward/backward-like kernel runs that touch weight shards to measure raw inter-GPU traffic depending on stride mapping.
2) Full inference benchmark: transformer decoder 7B-ish quantized shim with TP=2, DP=2 (4 GPUs) and TP=4, DP=1 (4 GPUs) topologies. Run identical prompt mix.
3) NCCL traces (NCCL_PROTO, NCCL_DEBUG) and nvprof / Nsight counters for interconnect utilization, packet sizes, and collective latency distribution.
4) Compare three placement strategies: contiguous, round-robin, stride-aware (manual mapping to reduce hop distance for frequent shard pairs).

Cluster config and workload:
- Machines: 4x A100-80GB per node, connected with NVSwitch inside node; two nodes per test (8 GPUs total) for cross-node experiments. Also single-node 4-GPU runs for intra-node effects.
- Topologies tested: intra-node NVSwitch (4 GPUs), 2-node NVLink+IB (8 GPUs) 
- Runtime: Redwood serving runtime build: feat/placement-probe (GH PR above). Kernel config: attention fused kernels, quantized GEMM path.
- Model: decoder-only 7.1B with 2048 context, 32 layers, standard MLP/attention. Quantized to 4-bit (smooth quant).
- Latency SLO target: p95 < 220ms for prompt length=64, throughput measured as tokens/s during sustained 300s run.

Placement strategies (what we tried):
- contiguous: shards 0..N mapped to GPUs 0..G consecutively (default).
- rr (round-robin): shards assigned mod G (0,1,2,... wrap).
- stride-aware (manual): we inspect layer access patterns and map consecutive layers that frequently exchange KV-cache across nearby indices. For example, map shard order [0,2,1,3] in a 4-GPU DP chunk so that heavy exchange pairs sit on same NVSwitch island when possible.

Microbench results (single-step, normalized):
- Metric: aggregate inter-GPU traffic (GB/s), collective latency median (us), small-packet ratio (>70% packets under 1KB).
- contiguous: 78 GB/s inter-GPU, coll median 210us, small-packet ratio 62%
- rr: 85 GB/s inter-GPU, coll median 240us, small-packet ratio 68%
- stride-aware: 61 GB/s inter-GPU, coll median 165us, small-packet ratio 48%
Observations: stride-aware mapping reduced aggregate cross-link traffic by ~20-25% and lowered median collective latency. The small-packet ratio dropped — implying more efficient packetization (fewer microbursts).

Full inference benchmark (TP=2,DP=2, 4 GPU logical shard vs TP=4,DP=1):
- Setup: identical request mix (single-turn sampling, top-p 0.9, temp 0.8), warmup 120s, measurement 300s.
- contiguous TP=2/DP=2: 10.4k tok/s sustained, p95 latency 210ms, CPU host-staging spikes observed every 8s.
- rr TP=2/DP=2: 9.6k tok/s sustained, p95 235ms, more frequent NCCL retries observed in logs.
- stride-aware TP=2/DP=2: 12.6k tok/s sustained, p95 190ms, host staging microbursts less frequent and smaller magnitude.
- contiguous TP=4/DP=1: 13.1k tok/s sustained, p95 170ms (single-node runs slightly better due to NVSwitch locality).
- stride-aware TP=4/DP=1: 14.0k tok/s sustained, p95 165ms

Key signal: stride-aware placement improved sustained throughput in our hybrid topologies by ~15-20% vs contiguous, and reduced p95 by ~10-12%. The benefit is larger when the topology includes cross-node hops (NVLink->IB) because mapping reduces long-hop collectives.

NCCL / interconnect traces notes:
- Under contiguous and rr we saw periodic AllReduce stalls where a single rank lagged by a few 100s of microseconds causing pipeline backpressure. These stalls aligned to a subset of layers whose shards mapped to remote GPUs across nodes, suggesting queuing on the cross-node link.
- stride-aware mapping smoothed the transfer schedule: collectives became more symmetric and average packet sizes increased (fewer tiny packets). Packetization behavior seems dominated by the fragmentation caused when discontiguous shards force many small send ops.
- NCCL logs: fewer NCCL_COLL_RETRY events under stride-aware and fewer "P2P_TIMEOUT" warnings in extreme rr case.

Host-side staging behavior:
- We noticed that contiguous mapping caused host transfer bursts at layer boundaries: large host->device DMA spikes followed by short quiescent periods. This pattern increased CPU interrupt contention. stride-aware mapping spread DMA more evenly across GPUs/time, reducing instantaneous host bottlenecks.

Hypothesis (mechanistic):
- Transformer inference frequently accesses a small set of adjacent parameter shards per layer (attention weights, MLP kernel pairs). If those adjacent shards are placed across devices that are topologically distant, the runtime issues many small cross-device sends leading to small-packet microbursts, high per-packet overhead, NCCL schedule tail growth, and host staging spikes.
- Placing frequently-interacting shards near each other (by hop distance) reduces cross-link hops and allows NCCL to create larger, more efficient packets and reduce synchronization skew.

Recommendations (short-term):
1) Implement an opt-in "stride-aware" placement heuristic in the scheduler that:
   - collects a quick access-frequency map during model load (or from profiling hints),
   - clusters high-interaction shards and assigns them to the same switch domain when possible,
   - falls back to contiguous/rr based on capacity constraints.
2) Add a CI microbenchmark that exercises different stride patterns to catch regressions in placements when models or quantization paths change.
3) Tune NCCL packetization parameters for workloads with high small-packet ratios (we saw wins increasing NCCL_PROTO_BUF_SIZE in some tests).
4) Add runtime telemetry: per-collective hop count and small-packet fraction exposed to Console for quick debugging.

Open questions / risks / TODOs:
- Is stride-aware always beneficial? We saw one weird case (very large batch sizes >512 tokens combined) where rr slightly outperformed stride-aware — likely because rr balanced per-GPU memory bandwidth better for extreme packing. We need an automated selector rather than a single policy.
- Interaction with model parallel schedules generated by our compiler (when we fuse or remap linear kernels) — ensure the placement heuristic respects the compiler's expected locality.
- Need to verify on other GPU families (H100) and on NVSwitch-heavy pods with 8+ GPUs per node. Current tests are skewed toward A100 and small-node topologies.
- Edge-case: multi-tenant nodes where we cannot co-locate shards due to isolation. How to best approximate?

Repro steps (quick):
1) Checkout runtime branch feat/placement-probe, build container image (instructions in GH PR).
2) Start 2-node cluster with identical firmware drivers. Use the attached run script (gh pr) to launch the benchmark with flags: --placement-policy {contiguous,rr,stride} --tp 2 --dp 2 --quant 4bit --meas 300s
3) Collect logs: /var/log/redwood/nccl-debug.log and runtime trace: /tmp/placement-probe-trace.{rank}.json and perf counters with counter set: PCI_BYTES, PACKET_SIZE_HIST, NVLINK_OPS.
4) Compare aggregated metrics via the helper script bench/compare_placement.py (in GH PR)

Artifacts attached in PR/Confluence and raw traces: see linked_artifacts above. I uploaded a small sampling of NCCL logs and the flamegraph under the PR for quick triage.

Notes to self / follow-ups for next week:
- Add automated heuristic that picks placement based on measured small-packet ratio during warmup phase.
- Experiment: try remapping only every N layers (coarse clustering) to reduce scheduler complexity.
- Performance model: start simple regression model to predict throughput from small-packet ratio + avg hop count + CPU-staging rate. Use it to pick placement policy at model load time.

Unresolved items to handoff to runtime compiler team:
- Need guarantee that if we instruct a stride-aware mapping, kernel fusion won't silently reassign logical shards in a way that breaks locality. Put a contract in the layout API.

Appendix: quick logs/snippets (sanitized)
- sample NCCL debug snippet: "[2026-02-17T12:04:34Z] Rank 2 waiting on ring 1: schedule skew 310us -> retry" (appeared 18x in contiguous run)
- sample perf counters: contiguous: NVLINK_BYTES=78.2GB/s, stride-aware: NVLINK_BYTES=61.3GB/s

If this looks useful I can:
- turn the stride-aware prototype into an experimental flag on dedicated pods,
- add a small Console dashboard tile (p95 vs placement policy) for controlled experiments, and
- schedule a cross-team sync (compiler + serving runtime + SRE) to formalize the placement contract.

Signed-off-by: Alyssa (notes-during-experiment).
